## Support Plan Meeting

This plan describes the supports to be delivered to the participant and how support workers are to deliver them. It must be read together with the participant's NDIS plan, service agreement, and any behaviour support plan, health support plan or risk assessment referenced in it.

**Participant Name:** Michael Rocca

**Date of Birth:** 24/08/1975

**Gender:** Male

**Language Spoken:** not recorded in retrieved evidence

**NDIS Number:** 430324461

**Diagnosis:** Moderate Intellectual Disability, Schizoaffective Disorder, Mixed Personality Disorder, and traits of autism spectrum disorder

**People Present:** not recorded in retrieved evidence

**Support Plan Developed By:** not recorded in retrieved evidence

**Plan Date:** 2026-10-05

**Date for Review:** To be confirmed by approver

## Goals

Goals are drawn from the participant's NDIS plan and from what the participant says matters to them. NDIS plan goals and personal goals are recorded together in the table below.

| Current situation | Goal | Actions | Person responsible | Timeframe | Outcomes |
|-------------------|------|---------|-------------------|-----------|----------|
| Not assessed — no functional assessment on file | Michael wants to manage his emotions better and appreciates when people give him time, explain things clearly, and include him in decisions that affect his day. | Support staff to provide feedback to Behaviour Support Practitioner. Goals to be tracked using GAS. | Support staff | To be confirmed by approver | Michael will demonstrate improved emotional regulation by using coping strategies when feeling overwhelmed. |
| Not assessed — no functional assessment on file | Michael aims to engage more in community activities such as going for a drive or having a meal. | Support staff to encourage participation in community outings. | Support staff | To be confirmed by approver | Michael will participate in at least one community activity per week. |
| Not assessed — no functional assessment on file | Michael wants to improve his personal hygiene routine. | Support staff to assist with daily hygiene tasks and encourage independence. | Support staff | To be confirmed by approver | Michael will independently complete his personal hygiene routine at least 3 times a week. |

## About Me

This section is about who the participant is, not what they cannot do. It is written to help a support worker understand the person before their first shift.

**Strengths:** Sociable, responds well to praise, validation and clear communication, humour, resilience, keeps his house tidy with support.  
**Likes:** Branded shoes, listening to music, Holden cars, keeping a tidy house, shopping.  
**Dislikes:** Being told what to do, being told he can’t do something, being alone, feeling rejected, feeling bored.  
**What matters to me:** Michael values independence, music, shopping, and outdoor activities, thriving on predictability and routine.  
**How I prefer to communicate:** Michael communicates verbally in English, prefers short, clear sentences, and benefits from visual aids.  
**People who matter to me:** [Insert names]  
**Informal supports:** [Insert details]

## History and Background

This section carries only the background a support worker needs to deliver safe, respectful support. It is not a clinical or case history. Every statement must be traceable to a named source document.

**Relevant History:** Michael’s behavioural challenges began in early childhood and have remained consistent across his life. He has displayed physical aggression, threats, assaults, and property damage. His interactions within the community have raised concerns regarding boundaries, especially in relation to children.  
**Prior Service Involvement:** Michael currently lives in Supported Independent Living (SIL) with 24-hour support. He has a complex health profile and requires consistent, long-term staff who build trust and rapport.  
**Risk-Relevant Context:** Michael has a history of trauma, including family violence and disrupted attachments, contributing to anxiety and mood instability. He has ongoing sleep issues and significant anxiety, leading to frequent use of medical and emergency services.  
**Source Documents and Dates:** 20260324 MR NDIS CBSP (Updated Sexualised Behaviour), dated 24/03/2023; Client Fire Risk Assessment Form_MR, dated 19/02/2026.

## Communication and Communication Strategy

Every worker must read and follow the communication strategy before their first shift with this participant. Communication difficulty is not a reason to make decisions on the participant's behalf. Where the participant uses a communication aid or system, it must be available and used at every shift.

**Verbal / Non-verbal:** Michael communicates verbally in English, although he has stated he doesn't know Italian that well. At his baseline, when calm and comfortable, Michael is polite, articulate and considerate.

**Expressive Capacity:** Michael responds best when spoken to using short, clear sentences and is more successful with directions when they are broken down into simple steps supported by visual aids.

**Receptive Capacity:** Difficulties in communication are compounded by cognitive challenges, limited vocabulary, attention difficulties, and a lack of functional literacy and numeracy. These challenges impact his ability to manage budgeting, time, and waiting.

**Communication Aid or System Used:** Michael has been introduced to Talking Mats to support his self-awareness around his likes, dislikes, and appropriate behaviours.

**Communication Strategy:** Workers should gain Michael's attention by using his name and making eye contact. Allow sufficient time for him to respond, and be aware of signs indicating whether he has understood, such as nodding or verbal acknowledgment. Avoid overwhelming him with too much information at once.

## Support Delivery and Client Safety

Supports are delivered only as funded in the participant's service agreement and NDIS plan. Workers must not deliver supports outside those recorded here without authorisation from the service manager. Incidents affecting the participant must be reported to the service manager immediately and recorded in the provider's incident management system before the end of shift. Where an incident meets the NDIS reportable incident criteria, the provider must submit an Immediate Notification Form to the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission within 24 hours of key personnel becoming aware of it. The exception is the use of a restrictive practice that is unauthorised or not in accordance with the participant's behaviour support plan, which is notified within five business days — unless it resulted in harm, in which case the 24-hour timeframe applies. In an emergency, call 000 first, then notify the on-call service manager. For non-emergency concerns about the participant's wellbeing, contact the service manager the same day.

## Behavioural Management

**Proactive strategies**

| Behaviour or trigger | Strategy | What the worker does | BSP source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Community access where children may be present | Supervised community access near children | Plan and supervise community access so Michael is supported in environments where children may be present; redirect or leave if risk increases. | 20260324 MR NDIS CBSP (Updated Sexualised Behaviour) (53cff928-61eb-4570-b5ad-55de23d3ea6e): • Ensure Michael’s community access is supported and supervised where required, particularly in environments where children may be present. |

**Reactive strategies**

| Behaviour or trigger | Strategy | What the worker does | BSP source |

| Post-incident reflection | Post-incident reflection after calm | Wait until Michael is calm, then briefly reflect on what happened, validate feelings, and identify one practical next step for next time. | 20260324 MR NDIS CBSP (Updated Sexualised Behaviour) (53cff928-61eb-4570-b5ad-55de23d3ea6e): • Encourage post-incident reflection with Michael (when calm) to build emotional understanding and relational trust. |

This section records what workers do with Michael in an emergency or evacuation. It supplements, and does not replace, the site emergency plan.

Source risk assessment: Client Fire Risk Assessment Form_MR.

**Worker strategy:**

In any emergency, worker priority is immediate safety. Call 000 first, maintain clear access to exits, and notify the on-call service manager after immediate safety actions are underway. Use only the recorded disaster-management values above: evacuation assistance required = not recorded in retrieved evidence; communication approach = not recorded in retrieved evidence; equipment present = Fire extinguisher, Smoke alarm. Do not add evacuation assistance, medication, equipment, assembly-point or communication requirements that are not recorded in the table.

substantiveBreakdown.countedContent: Every worker must read and follow the communication strategy before their first shift with this participant. Communication difficulty is not a reason to make decisions on the participant's behalf. Where the participant uses a communication aid or system, it must be available and used at every shift. **Verbal / Non-verbal:** Michael communicates verbally in English, although he has stated he doesn't know Italian that well. At his baseline, when calm and comfortable, Michael is polite, articulate and considerate. **Expressive Capacity:** Michael responds best when spoken to using short, clear sentences and is more successful with directions when they are broken down into simple steps supported by visual aids. **Receptive Capacity:** Difficulties in communication are compounded by cognitive challenges, limited vocabulary, attention difficulties, and a lack of functional literacy and numeracy. These challenges impact his ability to manage budgeting, time, and waiting. **Communication Aid or System Used:** Michael has been introduced to Talking Mats to support his self-awareness around his likes, dislikes, and appropriate behaviours. **Communication Strategy:** Workers should gain Michael's attention by using his name and making eye contact. Allow sufficient time for him to respond, and be aware of signs indicating whether he has understood, such as nodding or verbal acknowledgment. Avoid overwhelming him with too much information at once.

sections.content:
Support is provided to build and maintain independence. Workers do for the participant only what the participant cannot do for themselves at that time. Where the participant's capacity changes, the change is recorded and the plan updated.

Each activity below is recorded against one support level. Where an activity requires a specific strategy, that strategy is recorded in the section that governs it — mobility and transfers in Mobility and Mobility Strategy, meal preparation and eating in Mealtime Management Strategy, and medication in the participant's health support plan. This section records the level of support required, not the clinical or specialist strategy.

Support levels: Independent — completes the activity safely and effectively without assistance. Independent with prompting — physically completes the activity but requires verbal, visual or gestural prompts, reminders or task initiation. Independent with supervision — completes the activity but requires another person to remain available or observe for safety. Partial physical assistance — completes part of the activity but requires hands-on assistance for specific components. Full physical assistance — requires hands-on support for most or all of the activity. Unable to complete — cannot currently undertake the activity, even with ordinary prompting or supervision, without another person completing it. Not applicable / not assessed — activity is not relevant or sufficient information is unavailable.

sections.content:
Every worker must read and follow the communication strategy before their first shift with this participant. Communication difficulty is not a reason to make decisions on the participant's behalf. Where the participant uses a communication aid or system, it must be available and used at every shift.

**Verbal / Non-verbal:** Michael communicates verbally in English, although he has stated he doesn't know Italian that well. At his baseline, when calm and comfortable, Michael is polite, articulate and considerate.

**Expressive Capacity:** Michael responds best when spoken to using short, clear sentences and is more successful with directions when they are broken down into simple steps supported by visual aids.

**Receptive Capacity:** Difficulties in communication are compounded by cognitive challenges, limited vocabulary, attention difficulties, and a lack of functional literacy and numeracy. These challenges impact his ability to manage budgeting, time, and waiting.

**Communication Aid or System Used:** Michael has been introduced to Talking Mats to support his self-awareness around his likes, dislikes, and appropriate behaviours.

**Communication Strategy:** Workers should gain Michael's attention by using his name and making eye contact. Allow sufficient time for him to respond, and be aware of signs indicating whether he has understood, such as nodding or verbal acknowledgment. Avoid overwhelming him with too much information at once.

sections.content: Supports are delivered only as funded in the participant's service agreement and NDIS plan. Workers must not deliver supports outside those recorded here without authorisation from the service manager. Incidents affecting the participant must be reported to the service manager immediately and recorded in the provider's incident management system before the end of shift. Where an incident meets the NDIS reportable incident criteria, the provider must submit an Immediate Notification Form to the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission within 24 hours of key personnel becoming aware of it. The exception is the use of a restrictive practice that is unauthorised or not in accordance with the participant's behaviour support plan, which is notified within five business days — unless it resulted in harm, in which case the 24-hour timeframe applies. In an emergency, call 000 first, then notify the on-call service manager. For non-emergency concerns about the participant's wellbeing, contact the service manager the same day.

Every worker must read and follow the communication strategy before their first shift with this participant. Communication difficulty is not a reason to make decisions on the participant's behalf. Where the participant uses a communication aid or system, it must be available and used at every shift.

**Verbal / Non-verbal:** Michael communicates verbally in English, although he has stated he doesn't know Italian that well. At his baseline, when calm and comfortable, Michael is polite, articulate and considerate.

**Expressive Capacity:** Michael responds best when spoken to using short, clear sentences and is more successful with directions when they are broken down into simple steps supported by visual aids.

**Receptive Capacity:** Difficulties in communication are compounded by cognitive challenges, limited vocabulary, attention difficulties, and a lack of functional literacy and numeracy. These challenges impact his ability to manage budgeting, time, and waiting.

**Communication Aid or System Used:** Michael has been introduced to Talking Mats to support his self-awareness around his likes, dislikes, and appropriate behaviours.

**Communication Strategy:** Workers should gain Michael's attention by using his name and making eye contact. Allow sufficient time for him to respond, and be aware of signs indicating whether he has understood, such as nodding or verbal acknowledgment. Avoid overwhelming him with too much information at once.

He has a complex health profile and requires consistent, long-term staff who build trust and rapport. **Risk-Relevant Context:** Michael has a history of trauma, including family violence and disrupted attachments, contributing to anxiety and mood instability. He has ongoing sleep issues and significant anxiety, leading to frequent use of medical and emergency services. **Source Documents and Dates:** 20260324 MR NDIS CBSP (Updated Sexualised Behaviour), dated 24/03/2023; Client Fire Risk Assessment Form_MR, dated 19/02/2026.

substantiveBreakdown.countedContent: Every worker must read and follow the communication strategy before their first shift with this participant. Communication difficulty is not a reason to make decisions on the participant's behalf. Where the participant uses a communication aid or system, it must be available and used at every shift. **Verbal / Non-verbal:** Michael communicates verbally in English, although he has stated he doesn't know Italian that well. At his baseline, when calm and comfortable, Michael is polite, articulate and considerate. **Expressive Capacity:** Michael responds best when spoken to using short, clear sentences and is more successful with directions when they are broken down into simple steps supported by visual aids. **Receptive Capacity:** Difficulties in communication are compounded by cognitive challenges, limited vocabulary, attention difficulties, and a lack of functional literacy and numeracy. These challenges impact his ability to manage budgeting, time, and waiting. **Communication Aid or System Used:** Michael has been introduced to Talking Mats to support his self-awareness around his likes, dislikes, and appropriate behaviours. **Communication Strategy:** Workers should gain Michael's attention by using his name and making eye contact. Allow sufficient time for him to respond, and be aware of signs indicating whether he has understood, such as nodding or verbal acknowledgment. Avoid overwhelming him with too much information at once.

## Support Delivery and Client Safety

Supports are delivered only as funded in the participant's service agreement and NDIS plan. Workers must not deliver supports outside those recorded here without authorisation from the service manager. Incidents affecting the participant must be reported to the service manager immediately and recorded in the provider's incident management system before the end of shift. Where an incident meets the NDIS reportable incident criteria, the provider must submit an Immediate Notification Form to the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission within 24 hours of key personnel becoming aware of it. The exception is the use of a restrictive practice that is unauthorised or not in accordance with the participant's behaviour support plan, which is notified within five business days — unless it resulted in harm, in which case the 24-hour timeframe applies. In an emergency, call 000 first, then notify the on-call service manager. For non-emergency concerns about the participant's wellbeing, contact the service manager the same day.

substantiveBreakdown.countedContent: Every worker must read and follow the communication strategy before their first shift with this participant. Communication difficulty is not a reason to make decisions on the participant's behalf. Where the participant uses a communication aid or system, it must be available and used at every shift. **Verbal / Non-verbal:** Michael communicates verbally in English, although he has stated he doesn't know Italian that well. At his baseline, when calm and comfortable, Michael is polite, articulate and considerate. **Expressive Capacity:** Michael responds best when spoken to using short, clear sentences and is more successful with directions when they are broken down into simple steps supported by visual aids. **Receptive Capacity:** Difficulties in communication are compounded by cognitive challenges, limited vocabulary, attention difficulties, and a lack of functional literacy and numeracy. Allow sufficient time for him to respond, and be aware of signs indicating whether he has understood, such as nodding or verbal acknowledgment. Avoid overwhelming him with too much information at once.

This section is about who the participant is, not what they cannot do. It is written to help a support worker understand the person before their first shift.

**Strengths:** Sociable, responds well to praise, validation and clear communication, humour, resilience, keeps his house tidy with support.  
**Likes:** Branded shoes, listening to music, Holden cars, keeping a tidy house, shopping.  
**Dislikes:** Being told what to do, being told he can’t do something, being alone, feeling rejected, feeling bored.  
**What matters to me:** Michael values independence, music, shopping, and outdoor activities, thriving on predictability and routine.  
**How I prefer to communicate:** Michael communicates verbally in English, prefers short, clear sentences, and benefits from visual aids.

This section carries only the background a support worker needs to deliver safe, respectful support. It is not a clinical or case history. Every statement must be traceable to a named source document.

**Relevant History:** Michael’s behavioural challenges began in early childhood and have remained consistent across his life. He has displayed physical aggression, threats, assaults, and property damage. His interactions within the community have raised concerns regarding boundaries, especially in relation to children.  
**Prior Service Involvement:** Michael currently lives in Supported Independent Living (SIL) with 24-hour support. He has a complex health profile and requires consistent, long-term staff who build trust and rapport.  
**Risk-Relevant Context:** Michael has a history of trauma, including family violence and disrupted attachments, contributing to anxiety and mood instability. He has ongoing sleep issues and significant anxiety, leading to frequent use of medical and emergency services.  
**Source Documents and Dates:** 20260324 MR NDIS CBSP (Updated Sexualised Behaviour), dated 24/03/2023; Client Fire Risk Assessment Form_MR, dated 19/02/2026.

Support is provided to build and maintain independence. Workers do for the participant only what the participant cannot do for themselves at that time. Where the participant's capacity changes, the change is recorded and the plan updated.

Each activity below is recorded against one support level. Where an activity requires a specific strategy, that strategy is recorded in the section that governs it — mobility and transfers in Mobility and Mobility Strategy, meal preparation and eating in Mealtime Management Strategy, and medication in the participant's health support plan. This section records the level of support required, not the clinical or specialist strategy.

Support levels: Independent — completes the activity safely and effectively without assistance. Independent with prompting — physically completes the activity but requires verbal, visual or gestural prompts, reminders or task initiation. Independent with supervision — completes the activity but requires another person to remain available or observe for safety. Partial physical assistance — completes part of the activity but requires hands-on assistance for specific components. Full physical assistance — requires hands-on support for most or all of the activity. Unable to complete — cannot currently undertake the activity, even with ordinary prompting or supervision, without another person completing it. Not applicable / not assessed — activity is not relevant or sufficient information is unavailable.

Where the participant uses a communication aid or system, it must be available and used at every shift.

**Verbal / Non-verbal:** Michael communicates verbally in English, although he has stated he doesn't know Italian that well. At his baseline, when calm and comfortable, Michael is polite, articulate and considerate.

**Expressive Capacity:** Michael responds best when spoken to using short, clear sentences and is more successful with directions when they are broken down into simple steps supported by visual aids.

## Communication and Communication Strategy

Every worker must read and follow the communication strategy before their first shift with this participant. Communication difficulty is not a reason to make decisions on the participant's behalf. Where the participant uses a communication aid or system, it must be available and used at every shift. **Verbal / Non-verbal:** Michael communicates verbally in English, although he has stated he doesn't know Italian that well. At his baseline, when calm and comfortable, Michael is polite, articulate and considerate. **Expressive Capacity:** Michael responds best when spoken to using short, clear sentences and is more successful with directions when they are broken down into simple steps supported by visual aids. **Receptive Capacity:** Difficulties in communication are compounded by cognitive challenges, limited vocabulary, attention difficulties, and a lack of functional literacy and numeracy. These challenges impact his ability to manage budgeting, time, and waiting. **Communication Aid or System Used:** Michael has been introduced to Talking Mats to support his self-awareness around his likes, dislikes, and appropriate behaviours. **Communication Strategy:** Workers should gain Michael's attention by using his name and making eye contact. Allow sufficient time for him to respond, and be aware of signs indicating whether he has understood, such as nodding or verbal acknowledgment. Avoid overwhelming him with too much information at once.

## Support Delivery and Client Safety

Supports are delivered only as funded in the participant's service agreement and NDIS plan. Workers must not deliver supports outside those recorded here without authorisation from the service manager. Incidents affecting the participant must be reported to the service manager immediately and recorded in the provider's incident management system before the end of shift. Where an incident meets the NDIS reportable incident criteria, the provider must submit an Immediate Notification Form to the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission within 24 hours of key personnel becoming aware of it. The exception is the use of a restrictive practice that is unauthorised or not in accordance with the participant's behaviour support plan, which is notified within five business days — unless it resulted in harm, in which case the 24-hour timeframe applies. In an emergency, call 000 first, then notify the on-call service manager. For non-emergency concerns about the participant's wellbeing, contact the service manager the same day.

## Support Plan Meeting

This plan describes the supports to be delivered to the participant and how support workers are to deliver them. It must be read together with the participant's NDIS plan, service agreement, and any behaviour support plan, health support plan or risk assessment referenced in it. **Participant Name:** Michael Rocca **Date of Birth:** 24/08/1975 **Gender:** Male **Language Spoken:** not recorded in retrieved evidence **NDIS Number:** 430324461 **Diagnosis:** Moderate Intellectual Disability, Schizoaffective Disorder, Mixed Personality Disorder, and traits of autism spectrum disorder **People Present:** not recorded in retrieved evidence **Support Plan Developed By:** not recorded in retrieved evidence **Plan Date:** 2026-10-05 **Date for Review:** To be confirmed by approver

## Goals

Goals are drawn from the participant's NDIS plan and from what the participant says matters to them. NDIS plan goals and personal goals are recorded together in the table below. | Current situation | Goal | Actions | Person responsible | Timeframe | Outcomes |
|-------------------|------|---------|-------------------|-----------|----------|
| Not assessed — no functional assessment on file | Michael wants to manage his emotions better and appreciates when people give him time, explain things clearly, and include him in decisions that affect his day. | Support staff to provide feedback to Behaviour Support Practitioner. Goals to be tracked using GAS. | Support staff | not recorded in retrieved evidence | Michael will demonstrate improved emotional regulation by using coping strategies when feeling overwhelmed. |
| Not assessed — no functional assessment on file | Michael aims to engage more in community activities such as going for a drive or having a meal. | Support staff to encourage participation in community outings. | Support staff | not recorded in retrieved evidence | Michael will participate in at least one community activity per week. |
| Not assessed — no functional assessment on file | Michael wants to improve his personal hygiene routine. | Support staff to assist with daily hygiene tasks and encourage independence. | Support staff | not recorded in retrieved evidence | Michael will independently complete his personal hygiene routine at least 3 times a week. |

## About Me

This section is about who the participant is, not what they cannot do. It is written to help a support worker understand the person before their first shift. **Strengths:** Sociable, responds well to praise, validation and clear communication, humour, resilience, keeps his house tidy with support. **Likes:** Branded shoes, listening to music, Holden cars, keeping a tidy house, shopping. **Dislikes:** Being told what to do, being told he can’t do something, being alone, feeling rejected, feeling bored. **What matters to me:** Michael values independence, music, shopping, and outdoor activities, thriving on predictability and routine. **How I prefer to communicate:** Michael communicates verbally in English, prefers short, clear sentences, and benefits from visual aids. **People who matter to me:** not recorded in retrieved evidence **Informal supports:** not recorded in retrieved evidence

## History and Background

This section carries only the background a support worker needs to deliver safe, respectful support. It is not a clinical or case history. Every statement must be traceable to a named source document. **Relevant History:** Michael’s behavioural challenges began in early childhood and have remained consistent across his life. He has displayed physical aggression, threats, assaults, and property damage. His interactions within the community have raised concerns regarding boundaries, especially in relation to children. **Prior Service Involvement:** Michael currently lives in Supported Independent Living (SIL) with 24-hour support. He has a complex health profile and requires consistent, long-term staff who build trust and rapport. **Risk-Relevant Context:** Michael has a history of trauma, including family violence and disrupted attachments, contributing to anxiety and mood instability. He has ongoing sleep issues and significant anxiety, leading to frequent use of medical and emergency services. **Source Documents and Dates:** 20260324 MR NDIS CBSP (Updated Sexualised Behaviour), dated 24/03/2023; Client Fire Risk Assessment Form_MR, dated 19/02/2026.

## Communication and Communication Strategy

Every worker must read and follow the communication strategy before their first shift with this participant. Communication difficulty is not a reason to make decisions on the participant's behalf. Where the participant uses a communication aid or system, it must be available and used at every shift. **Verbal / Non-verbal:** Michael communicates verbally in English, although he has stated he doesn't know Italian that well. At his baseline, when calm and comfortable, Michael is polite, articulate and considerate. **Expressive Capacity:** Michael responds best when spoken to using short, clear sentences and is more successful with directions when they are broken down into simple steps supported by visual aids. **Receptive Capacity:** Difficulties in communication are compounded by cognitive challenges, limited vocabulary, attention difficulties, and a lack of functional literacy and numeracy. These challenges impact his ability to manage budgeting, time, and waiting. **Communication Aid or System Used:** Michael has been introduced to Talking Mats to support his self-awareness around his likes, dislikes, and appropriate behaviours. **Communication Strategy:** Workers should gain Michael's attention by using his name and making eye contact. Allow sufficient time for him to respond, and be aware of signs indicating whether he has understood, such as nodding or verbal acknowledgment. Avoid overwhelming him with too much information at once.

## Support Delivery and Client Safety

Supports are delivered only as funded in the participant's service agreement and NDIS plan. substantiveBreakdown.countedContent: This section carries only the background a support worker needs to deliver safe, respectful support. It is not a clinical or case history. Every statement must be traceable to a named source document. **Relevant History:** Michael’s behavioural challenges began in early childhood and have remained consistent across his life. He has displayed physical aggression, threats, assaults, and property damage. His interactions within the community have raised concerns regarding boundaries, especially in relation to children. **Prior Service Involvement:** Michael currently lives in Supported Independent Living (SIL) with 24-hour support. He has a complex health profile and requires consistent, long-term staff who build trust and rapport. **Risk-Relevant Context:** Michael has a history of trauma, including family violence and disrupted attachments, contributing to anxiety and mood instability. He has ongoing sleep issues and significant anxiety, leading to frequent use of medical and emergency services. **Source Documents and Dates:** 20260324 MR NDIS CBSP (Updated Sexualised Behaviour), dated 24/03/2023; Client Fire Risk Assessment Form_MR, dated 19/02/2026.

substantiveBreakdown.countedContent: Every worker must read and follow the communication strategy before their first shift with this participant. Communication difficulty is not a reason to make decisions on the participant's behalf. Where the participant uses a communication aid or system, it must be available and used at every shift. **Verbal / Non-verbal:** Michael communicates verbally in English, although he has stated he doesn't know Italian that well. At his baseline, when calm and comfortable, Michael is polite, articulate and considerate. **Expressive Capacity:** Michael responds best when spoken to using short, clear sentences and is more successful with directions when they are broken down into simple steps supported by visual aids. **Receptive Capacity:** Difficulties in communication are compounded by cognitive challenges, limited vocabulary, attention difficulties, and a lack of functional literacy and numeracy. These challenges impact his ability to manage budgeting, time, and waiting. **Communication Aid or System Used:** Michael has been introduced to Talking Mats to support his self-awareness around his likes, dislikes, and appropriate behaviours. **Communication Strategy:** Workers should gain Michael's attention by using his name and making eye contact. Allow sufficient time for him to respond, and be aware of signs indicating whether he has understood, such as nodding or verbal acknowledgment. Avoid overwhelming him with too much information at once.

Support is provided to build and maintain independence. Workers do for the participant only what the participant cannot do for themselves at that time. Where the participant's capacity changes, the change is recorded and the plan updated. Each activity below is recorded against one support level. Where an activity requires a specific strategy, that strategy is recorded in the section that governs it — mobility and transfers in Mobility and Mobility Strategy, meal preparation and eating in Mealtime Management Strategy, and medication in the participant's health support plan. This section records the level of support required, not the clinical or specialist strategy. Support levels: Independent — completes the activity safely and effectively without assistance. Independent with prompting — physically completes the activity but requires verbal, visual or gestural prompts, reminders or task initiation. Independent with supervision — completes the activity but requires another person to remain available or observe for safety. Partial physical assistance — completes part of the activity but requires hands-on assistance for specific components. Full physical assistance — requires hands-on support for most or all of the activity. Unable to complete — cannot currently undertake the activity, even with ordinary prompting or supervision, without another person completing it. deliverableSections.content: Every worker must read and follow the communication strategy before their first shift with this participant. Communication difficulty is not a reason to make decisions on the participant's behalf. Where the participant uses a communication aid or system, it must be available and used at every shift. **Verbal / Non-verbal:** Michael communicates verbally in English, although he has stated he doesn't know Italian that well. At his baseline, when calm and comfortable, Michael is polite, articulate and considerate. **Expressive Capacity:** Michael responds best when spoken to using short, clear sentences and is more successful with directions when they are broken down into simple steps supported by visual aids. **Receptive Capacity:** Difficulties in communication are compounded by cognitive challenges, limited vocabulary, attention difficulties, and a lack of functional literacy and numeracy. These challenges impact his ability to manage budgeting, time, and waiting. **Communication Aid or System Used:** Michael has been introduced to Talking Mats to support his self-awareness around his likes, dislikes, and appropriate behaviours. **Communication Strategy:** Workers should gain Michael's attention by using his name and making eye contact. Allow sufficient time for him to respond, and be aware of signs indicating whether he has understood, such as nodding or verbal acknowledgment. Avoid overwhelming him with too much information at once.
deliverableSections.heading: Communication and Communication Strategy

deliverableSections.content: Supports are delivered only as funded in the participant's service agreement and NDIS plan. Workers must not deliver supports outside those recorded here without authorisation from the service manager. Incidents affecting the participant must be reported to the service manager immediately and recorded in the provider's incident management system before the end of shift. Where an incident meets the NDIS reportable incident criteria, the provider must submit an Immediate Notification Form to the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission within 24 hours of key personnel becoming aware of it. The exception is the use of a restrictive practice that is unauthorised or not in accordance with the participant's behaviour support plan, which is notified within five business days — unless it resulted in harm, in which case the 24-hour timeframe applies. In an emergency, call 000 first, then notify the on-call service manager. For non-emergency concerns about the participant's wellbeing, contact the service manager the same day.

## Communication and Communication Strategy

Every worker must read and follow the communication strategy before their first shift with this participant. Communication difficulty is not a reason to make decisions on the participant's behalf. Where the participant uses a communication aid or system, it must be available and used at every shift. **Verbal / Non-verbal:** Michael communicates verbally in English, although he has stated he doesn't know Italian that well. At his baseline, when calm and comfortable, Michael is polite, articulate and considerate. **Expressive Capacity:** Michael responds best when spoken to using short, clear sentences and is more successful with directions when they are broken down into simple steps supported by visual aids. **Receptive Capacity:** Difficulties in communication are compounded by cognitive challenges, limited vocabulary, attention difficulties, and a lack of functional literacy and numeracy. These challenges impact his ability to manage budgeting, time, and waiting. **Communication Aid or System Used:** Michael has been introduced to Talking Mats to support his self-awareness around his likes, dislikes, and appropriate behaviours. **Communication Strategy:** Workers should gain Michael's attention by using his name and making eye contact. Allow sufficient time for him to respond, and be aware of signs indicating whether he has understood, such as nodding or verbal acknowledgment. Avoid overwhelming him with too much information at once.

## Support Delivery and Client Safety

Supports are delivered only as funded in the participant's service agreement and NDIS plan. Workers must not deliver supports outside those recorded here without authorisation from the service manager. Incidents affecting the participant must be reported to the service manager immediately and recorded in the provider's incident management system before the end of shift. Where an incident meets the NDIS reportable incident criteria, the provider must submit an Immediate Notification Form to the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission within 24 hours of key personnel becoming aware of it. The exception is the use of a restrictive practice that is unauthorised or not in accordance with the participant's behaviour support plan, which is notified within five business days — unless it resulted in harm, in which case the 24-hour timeframe applies. In an emergency, call 000 first, then notify the on-call service manager. For non-emergency concerns about the participant's wellbeing, contact the service manager the same day.
